hearts.tree/josephus: Josephus, a Temple priest and Jewish commander who surrendered to Rome, wrote at Rome the histories that hold a few lines on John the Baptist, James and Jesus, which Christians copied for centuries as an outsider's word and argued over.
hearts.tree/tacitus: Tacitus, a Roman historian who despised the Christians, gave the fullest outside account of how Nero blamed them for the fire of 64 and killed them cruelly, and named Christ as put to death under Pilate.
hearts.tree/ignatius-of-antioch: Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, led in chains to die in the arena at Rome, wrote seven letters on the way urging the churches to keep together around their bishop, to hold that Christ truly suffered, and asking Rome not to save him.
hearts.tree/suetonius: Suetonius, a Roman writer of emperors' lives, left only two short lines that may touch the first Christians, a Claudius expulsion over "Chrestus" and a Nero punishment, which later Christians took up and joined to the Acts.
hearts.tree/valentinus: Valentinus, a teacher at Rome in the mid-second century, founded a school that taught heavenly powers coming forth in pairs and a world born from a fall; he is known almost only through the church writers who answered him with faith in one God who made the world.
hearts.tree/tatian: Tatian, a convert trained in Greek learning, scorned Greek wisdom as younger than Moses, left the church after Justin's death to found his own strict school, and wove the four Gospels into the Diatessaron, long read in the Syriac churches.
hearts.tree/clement-of-alexandria: Clement taught at Alexandria and answered Christians who feared Greek philosophy by arguing it might be God's gift to lead the Greeks to Christ, as the Law led the Hebrews.
hearts.tree/origen: Origen made his life's work the question of what Scripture means beneath its plain words; he taught at Alexandria and Caesarea, set the Hebrew beside the Greek, and his books were read and fought over for centuries.
hearts.tree/hippolytus-of-rome: Hippolytus, a Greek-writing teacher at Rome in the early 200s, held against Noetus and the bishops Zephyrinus and Callistus that the Son is another beside the Father yet one God with him, and resisted Callistus's forgiveness; exiled to Sardinia in 235, he was kept among Rome's martyrs.
hearts.tree/pontius-the-deacon: Pontius, Cyprian's deacon who shared his exile and his last night, wrote the Life and Passion of Cyprian so that later readers would have his bishop's example, and ended it grieving that he was left behind.
hearts.tree/anatolius-of-alexandria-and-laodice: Anatolius, a learned Christian of Alexandria, used a council vote to free almost all of a starving besieged quarter, later became bishop of Laodicea, and wrote an Easter rule that the Irish and Rome's defenders both claimed centuries on.
hearts.tree/pamphilus-of-caesarea: Pamphilus, a presbyter of Caesarea, built his church's library, copied and defended Origen's works, gave Scriptures freely, and was put to death as a martyr about 310.
hearts.tree/peter-of-alexandria: Peter, bishop of Alexandria in the Great Persecution, set out how the church should take back those who had fallen, weighing what each had suffered and chosen, faced Melitius's break, and was beheaded in 311.
hearts.tree/lactantius: Lactantius, teaching Latin rhetoric at Nicomedia when the Great Persecution began, answered with the Divine Institutes, arguing the faith to educated pagans from their own authorities and holding that religion cannot be forced, only defended by dying, not killing.
hearts.tree/methodius-of-olympus: Methodius, bishop of Olympus, praised the virgin life in the Banquet and argued against Origen in On the Resurrection that body and soul are one and the same body will rise.
